A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniBYD and UniManip and contain readable main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Content can be matched across relocation and renumbering. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation comparisons, ablations, training analyses, and real-world manipulation trials in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulation and real-world results, including revised benchmark scores, GRAB evaluation, and additional component and sensitivity studies.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.1 replaces v1's composite imitation-reward/success metric and complementary reward weights with a clipped success-based transition factor, an earliest-trigger threshold, and independently bounded reward weights. Section 6.2 also changes fixed initial PD gains to object-mass-scaled gains. Algorithm 1 reflects these procedural revisions; UMR and hand-action blending remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds GRAB evaluation and substantially revises UniManip's task selection. Figure 10 introduces tasks such as joystick retrieval and changes USB insertion to removal. Section 4.1 changes the morphology-specific category counts from 6/8/8/7 to 8/8/9/6, totaling 31 instead of 29. Appendix Section 10.2 inconsistently retains the old total.

E2.justification: The external baseline suite remains Retargeting, ManipTrans, and DexMachina*, with Only RL retained in Figure 11. New appendix comparisons introduce ablated comparators without morphological descriptors, boundary loss, entropy loss, or reward annealing. The newly nonzero bimanual baseline scores reflect changed results, not newly added external baselines.

E3.justification: The reported AS evaluation expands from Gemini 2.5 Pro and ten human raters to three model judges and 100 raters, with success-label blinding newly stated. Section 10.3 nevertheless retains the old recipe. Curriculum settings also change, and Section 14.2 introduces ±50% sensitivity sweeps. The 1,000 trials per task and physical success thresholds remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing SE/GR/LSC ablations and training analyses, v2 adds morphological-descriptor removal and training-efficiency analysis, curriculum hyperparameter sensitivity, and separate boundary-loss, entropy-loss, and reward-annealing ablations in Sections 14.1–14.3. Section 9.5 adds a failure-cause breakdown across 150 real-world trials.

E5.justification: Both versions retain ten repeated MLLM ratings in Section 10.3. Neither specifies independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The larger reported human panel changes the evaluation sample, without introducing a stated uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figure 5 substantially change. Table 1 replaces the 78.07% bimanual UniBYD success rate and near-zero baselines with 57.67% and 2.10%/28.75%/25.33% for Retargeting/ManipTrans/DexMachina*. GRAB adds 98.00% success, alongside new appendix results. Changed tasks and settings preclude same-setting performance conclusions. Real-world counts remain 26/50, 32/50, and 35/50.

T1.justification: The formal definitions of the curriculum performance factor and piecewise reward weights are revised in Section 3.2.1, and Section 6.2 adds the mass-scaling equations for PD gains. Other reward, UMR, PPO, retargeting, and failure-criterion mathematics remain substantially unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The core contributions remain a unified morphology-aware framework, learning beyond imitation, and the UniManip benchmark. The abstract and contribution list revise the reported headline success-rate advantage from 67.90% to 44.08%. The offline-informed/online-adaptive terminology largely reframes the retained imitation-to-exploration claim.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the earlier real-world transfer narrative: Section 9.5 discusses initialization and boundary loss as transfer mechanisms, acknowledges over 95% simulation success versus 62% real-world success, and explains collision, dropping, and joint-limit failures. It also positions AS as a qualitative complement and adds interpretations of component importance and hyperparameter robustness.

D1.justification: Section 9.5 newly documents RealSense D435i sensing, FoundationPose, calibrated hand–flange transforms, IK/RRT-Connect planning through MoveIt!, and 20 Hz policy execution. Table 4 supplies revised controller and reward parameters. These disclosures do not establish that deployment experiments were rerun. Both versions promise release upon acceptance, but v2 removes the repository address.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to GRAB and FoundationPose for the additional dataset evaluation and deployment description. The related-work discussion and positioning against imitation-centric and goal-centric manipulation methods otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, reward-annealing explanation, and experimental discussion receive substantial rewriting, emphasizing state drift and the offline-informed to online-adaptive narrative. Qualitative analysis becomes a separate Section 4.5, and deployment and supplementary analyses gain dedicated subsections. Much of the existing appendix reward explanation and prompting material remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 6 expands with additional examples and GRAB; Figure 10 is extensively redrawn as a large illustrated task map; Figure 5 receives replacement plots and revised display styling. Table 2 gains a full-UniBYD column, Table 4 expands, and Tables 6–7 are added. Existing appendix qualitative figures are largely retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful component tests, sensitivity analysis, deployment details, and explicit failure analysis. However, conflicting task totals and evaluator counts leave the revised evaluation ambiguous. New Table 7 also labels PE values of 0.10–0.20 as metres despite the 3 cm success threshold, without explanation. These reporting problems undermine confidence in the added evidence, leaving the net quality change uncertain.
